decks.title: Rate of Reaction and Rate Laws — Part 1: Rate, factors and rate laws
goals: Express average and instantaneous rates and relate the rates of change of different species
Explain slow and fast reactions in terms of bonds, and the effect of each factor on rate
State the law of mass action
Deduce order and rate constant from initial-rate data and derive the units of k

slides.heading: Rate of reaction
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how fast reactions go and how the rate depends on concentration.

rows: Fading of a dye in sunlight

visual.alt: Table of reactions with very different speeds

slides.narration: Namaste! Chemical kinetics is the study of how fast reactions go and the steps by which they happen. Thermodynamics tells us whether a reaction can happen; kinetics tells us how quickly. A silver chloride precipitate forms in an instant, while coal forms over millions of years. Kinetics helps industry choose conditions, doctors plan doses and food scientists keep food fresh.

slides.heading: Slow and fast reactions
slides.body_md: **Ionic reactions** in solution are very fast: ions are already free, and no bonds need to be broken, so they react on collision. **Molecular (covalent) reactions** are slower: covalent bonds must be broken and new ones formed, which needs energy and suitable orientation.

rows: Oppositely charged ions combine; no bond breaking
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl; H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
Decomposition of H₂O₂; hydrolysis of an ester
Rusting; H₂ + O₂ at room temperature

visual.alt: Table of fast, moderate and slow reactions explained by bonds

slides.narration: Why are some reactions so fast? When solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride are mixed, silver and chloride ions are already free and simply combine as they meet. In molecular reactions, strong covalent bonds have to be broken before new ones form, and that needs energy, so they go more slowly. Hydrogen and oxygen can stay mixed for years at room temperature.

slides.heading: Rate of reaction
slides.body_md: The **rate** is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. For $\mathrm{R} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}$, the **average rate** over an interval is $-\Delta[\ce{R}]/\Delta t = \Delta[\ce{P}]/\Delta t$; the minus sign makes the rate positive because $[\ce{R}]$ falls. Units: $\text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$; for gases, atm s⁻¹.

rows: Δ[R] is negative; rate must be positive
Reactants are used up, so most reactions slow down

visual.alt: Table of key points about the rate of reaction

slides.narration: The rate tells us how quickly a reactant’s concentration falls or a product’s rises. Because the reactant’s concentration decreases, we put a minus sign in front to keep the rate positive. Rates are usually given in moles per litre per second. Most reactions slow down as they go, because the reactants are being used up.

slides.heading: Average and instantaneous rate
slides.body_md: The **average rate** is the slope of a chord between two times. The **instantaneous rate** is minus the slope of the **tangent** to the concentration–time curve at that moment.

visual.alt: Concentration of a reactant falling along a curve from 0.6 towards zero over 50 seconds, with a straight tangent touching the curve at 15 seconds; the steepness of the tangent gives the instantaneous rate
visual.caption: Illustrative data. Instantaneous rate = −(slope of the tangent).

slides.narration: Here the reactant concentration falls along a curve. An average rate uses two points and hides what happens in between. To find the rate at one instant, say fifteen seconds, draw a tangent touching the curve there and measure its slope: the instantaneous rate is minus that slope. The curve is steepest at the start, when the reaction is fastest.

slides.heading: Rate in terms of each species
slides.body_md: For $\ce{aA + bB -> cC + dD}$, divide each rate of change by its coefficient to get **one** rate of reaction.

visual.alt: Table of relative rates for the synthesis of ammonia

slides.narration: In the synthesis of ammonia, hydrogen is used three times as fast as nitrogen, and ammonia forms twice as fast as nitrogen is used. To get a single rate for the reaction, we divide each rate of change by its coefficient, with a minus sign for the reactants. Then every species gives the same value.

slides.heading: Worked example: average rate and related rates
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2}$, $[\ce{N2O5}]$ falls from $0.240$ to $0.180\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ in $20\ \text{min}$. Find (a) the average rate of disappearance of N₂O₅, (b) the rate of reaction and (c) the rate of formation of NO₂.

**(a)** $-\Delta[\ce{N2O5}]/\Delta t = 0.060 \div 20 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$.

**(b)** Rate $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-3} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$.

**(c)** $\Delta[\ce{NO2}]/\Delta t = 4 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$.

headers: Rate of change / mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹

visual.alt: Table of rates for the decomposition of dinitrogen pentoxide

slides.narration: The concentration of dinitrogen pentoxide falls by six hundredths of a mole per litre in twenty minutes, three thousandths per minute. Dividing by its coefficient, two, gives the rate of the reaction itself, one and a half thousandths. Nitrogen dioxide, with a coefficient of four, forms four times as fast as that: six thousandths of a mole per litre per minute.

slides.heading: Quick check: relating rates
slides.body_md: Relate the rate of use of one species to the rate of formation of another.
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide each rate of change by its coefficient in the balanced equation; the results must be equal.

slides.heading: Factors affecting the rate
slides.body_md: The rate depends on the **nature of reactants**, **surface area**, **concentration**, **temperature**, a **catalyst** and **radiation** (light).

rows: AgCl precipitation vs burning of coal
Coal dust explosions; powdered zinc with acid
Charcoal burns faster in pure O₂
Rate roughly doubles for a 10 K rise
Food spoils faster outside a fridge
Fe in the Haber process; enzymes
Light supplies energy to start photochemical reactions
H₂ + Cl₂ explodes in sunlight; photosynthesis; fading of dyes

visual.alt: Table of factors affecting reaction rate with examples

slides.narration: Several factors change the rate. Ionic reactions are faster than molecular ones. Powders react faster than lumps because more surface is exposed. Higher concentration means more collisions. Raising the temperature by ten degrees roughly doubles many rates. A catalyst provides an easier path. And light can start photochemical reactions: a mixture of hydrogen and chlorine is stable in the dark but explodes in sunlight.

slides.heading: Law of mass action and active mass
slides.body_md: **Law of mass action** (Guldberg and Waage): at constant temperature, the rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the product of the **active masses** of the reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient. **Active mass** = molar concentration (mol L⁻¹) for solutions and gases; for pure solids and liquids it is taken as constant (unity).

rows: Strictly true only for elementary reactions

visual.alt: Table comparing the law of mass action with the experimental rate law

slides.narration: The law of mass action says that the rate is proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants, each raised to its coefficient. Active mass simply means molar concentration; for pure solids and liquids it is taken as one. The law is exact only for elementary reactions. For most real reactions, the powers in the rate law have to be found by experiment, as we see next.

slides.heading: Rate law, rate constant and order
slides.body_md: The **rate law** gives rate $= k[\ce{A}]^x[\ce{B}]^y$, with $x$ and $y$ found **by experiment**. The **rate constant** $k$ is the rate when all concentrations are 1 mol L⁻¹; it depends on temperature (and catalyst), not on concentration. **Order** $= x + y$; it may be 0, 1, 2, 3 or a fraction.

visual.alt: Table of reactions with experimental rate laws and orders

slides.narration: The rate law tells us how the rate depends on each concentration. The powers come from experiment, not from the balanced equation: dinitrogen pentoxide has a coefficient of two, yet its decomposition is first order; hydrogen and bromine give an order of one and a half. The rate constant is characteristic of the reaction at a given temperature. Adding the powers gives the overall order.

slides.heading: Units of the rate constant
slides.body_md: For an $n$th-order reaction, $k = \text{rate}/[\ce{A}]^n$, so its unit is $(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of units of the rate constant for orders zero to three

slides.narration: Because the rate always has units of moles per litre per second, the unit of k depends on the order. For zero order, k has the same unit as the rate; for first order, it is simply per second; for second order, litres per mole per second. So the unit of a rate constant reveals the order of the reaction.

slides.heading: Quick check: units of k
slides.body_md: Identify the order of a reaction from the unit of its rate constant.
slides.narration: Quick check. Per second alone means first order; moles per litre per second means zero order.

slides.heading: Worked example: method of initial rates
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{P + Q -> products}$ at 300 K:

| Expt | [P] / M | [Q] / M | Initial rate / M min⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.20 | 0.10 | 1.2 × 10⁻³ |
| 2 | 0.40 | 0.10 | 2.4 × 10⁻³ |
| 3 | 0.20 | 0.30 | 1.08 × 10⁻² |

**Step 1.** 1 → 2: [P] ×2, rate ×2 → first order in P.

**Step 2.** 1 → 3: [Q] ×3, rate ×9 → second order in Q. Rate $= k[\ce{P}][\ce{Q}]^2$; overall order 3.

**Step 3.** $k = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} \div (0.20 \times 0.10^2) = 0.60\ \text{L}^2\ \text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{min}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Flow for the method of initial rates

slides.narration: Compare experiments in which only one concentration changes. Doubling P doubles the rate, so the reaction is first order in P. Tripling Q multiplies the rate by nine, which is three squared, so it is second order in Q. Substituting any experiment gives k, nought point six, with units for a third-order reaction: litres squared per mole squared per minute.

slides.heading: Worked example: predicting a new rate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For rate $= k[\ce{P}][\ce{Q}]^2$, how does the rate change if [P] is halved and [Q] is tripled?

**Step 1.** Factor $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3^2 = 4.5$.

**Step 2.** The rate becomes $4.5$ times the original.

visual.alt: Table of the factors by which the rate changes

slides.narration: Treat each change as a factor raised to its own power. Halving P, which is first order, multiplies the rate by one half. Tripling Q, which is second order, multiplies it by nine. Together the rate goes up four and a half times. This factor method is quicker and safer than substituting numbers into the whole rate law.

slides.heading: Quick check: order from data
slides.body_md: Deduce the order with respect to a reactant from how the rate changes.
slides.narration: Quick check. If doubling a concentration multiplies the rate by four, the order in that reactant is two.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Ionic reactions are fast; reactions needing covalent bonds to break are slower.
Rate $= -\frac{1}{a}\frac{\Delta[\ce{A}]}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{c}\frac{\Delta[\ce{C}]}{\Delta t}$; instantaneous rate from the tangent.
Factors: nature, surface area, concentration, temperature, catalyst, radiation.
Law of mass action: rate ∝ product of active masses raised to their coefficients.
Rate law $k[\ce{A}]^x[\ce{B}]^y$ (experimental); order $= x + y$; unit of $k$ $= (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n}\text{s}^{-1}$.

rows: Change in concentration per unit time
Rate at unit concentrations; depends on T

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1 terms

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Reaction rates range from instant to geological, depending largely on whether bonds must be broken. The rate is the change in concentration per unit time, divided by the coefficient. It depends on several factors, including light. The law of mass action gives the idea of active mass, and the experimental rate law gives the order and the units of the rate constant.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Use a minus sign for reactants and divide by coefficients.
Never take orders from the balanced equation unless the reaction is elementary.
In initial-rate problems, compare runs where only one concentration changes.
State the unit of k with every value.

rows: Rate of reaction = rate of change of NO₂

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and fixes

slides.narration: A few tips. Always divide by coefficients and use a minus sign for reactants. Never assume orders from the balanced equation. In initial-rate problems, choose runs where only one concentration changes. And always write the unit of the rate constant.

decks.title: Rate of Reaction and Rate Laws — Part 2: Integrated rate laws, half-life and mechanism
goals: Use the integrated rate equation for a zero-order reaction and interpret its graph
Derive the integrated rate equation and half-life of a first-order reaction
Solve problems on rate constant, half-life and time for a given fraction to react
Distinguish order from molecularity and write the rate law from the slowest step of a mechanism

slides.heading: Concentration and time
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how concentration changes with time, and the steps by which reactions happen.

visual.alt: Flow of topics in Part 2

slides.narration: In Part 2 we answer practical questions. How long until half a drug has left the blood? How much pollutant remains after a day? To answer, we integrate the rate law to get concentration as a function of time for zero- and first-order reactions. Then we look inside reactions at their elementary steps and see how the slowest step controls the rate law.

slides.heading: Zero-order reactions
slides.body_md: Rate $= -\dfrac{d[\ce{R}]}{dt} = k$. Integrating from $[\ce{R}]_0$ at $t = 0$: $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0 - kt$. Half-life $t_{1/2} = [\ce{R}]_0/2k$ (proportional to the initial concentration). Examples: decomposition of NH₃ on hot platinum at high pressure; some enzyme reactions at saturation; H₂ + Cl₂ photochemical reaction.

visual.alt: Table of features of a zero-order reaction

slides.narration: In a zero-order reaction the rate does not depend on concentration. A gas decomposing on a fully covered hot metal surface is the classic case: adding more gas cannot make it go faster. So the concentration falls by the same amount every minute, giving a straight line. Its half-life is proportional to the starting concentration.

slides.heading: Zero order on a graph
slides.body_md: A plot of $[\ce{R}]$ against $t$ is a straight line with intercept $[\ce{R}]_0$ and slope $-k$; the reaction stops when the reactant is used up.

visual.alt: Zero-order reaction: the concentration falls in a straight line from 0.50 mol per litre to zero at 25 minutes; the slope is minus k
visual.caption: k = 0.02 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹ in this example.

slides.narration: Here the concentration starts at nought point five mole per litre and falls by two hundredths every minute, reaching zero at twenty five minutes. The graph is a straight line of slope minus k. Compare it with the curved first-order graph on the next slides.

slides.heading: Worked example: a zero-order reaction
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A zero-order reaction has $k = 0.025\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$. Starting at $[\ce{R}]_0 = 0.30\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$, find (a) $[\ce{R}]$ after 8 min, (b) the half-life and (c) the time for completion.

**(a)** $[\ce{R}] = 0.30 - 0.025 \times 8 = 0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

**(b)** $t_{1/2} = 0.30 \div (2 \times 0.025) = 6.0\ \text{min}$.

**(c)** $t = 0.30 \div 0.025 = 12\ \text{min}$.

visual.alt: Table of results of the zero-order example

slides.narration: For zero order the concentration simply falls by k every minute. After eight minutes it has fallen by nought point two, leaving nought point one. The half-life is the starting concentration divided by twice k, six minutes, and the reaction is complete after twelve minutes: exactly two half-lives, unlike a first-order reaction.

slides.heading: Quick check: zero order
slides.body_md: Recognise a zero-order reaction from its graph or half-life.
slides.narration: Quick check. For zero order, concentration falls in a straight line and the half-life is proportional to the starting concentration.

slides.heading: First-order reactions: derivation
slides.body_md: Rate $= -\dfrac{d[\ce{R}]}{dt} = k[\ce{R}]$. Separating variables, $\dfrac{d[\ce{R}]}{[\ce{R}]} = -k\,dt$. Integrating with $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0$ at $t = 0$: $\ln[\ce{R}] - \ln[\ce{R}]_0 = -kt$. Hence:

visual.alt: For a first-order reaction, a graph of log of concentration against time is a straight line sloping down; its slope equals minus k divided by 2.303
visual.caption: Illustrative: slope −0.03 min⁻¹, so k = 2.303 × 0.03 = 0.069 min⁻¹.

slides.narration: For a first-order reaction, the rate is k times the concentration. Rearranging puts all the concentration terms on one side and time on the other. Integrating from time zero gives the natural log of the starting concentration over the present concentration equal to k t. Converting to common logs introduces the factor two point three zero three. A graph of log concentration against time is a straight line with slope minus k over two point three zero three.

slides.heading: First-order decay and half-life
slides.body_md: The concentration falls exponentially and **halves in equal intervals of time**: the half-life $t_{1/2}$.

visual.alt: First-order decay: the concentration halves every 8 minutes, from 0.64 to 0.32, 0.16 and 0.08 at 8, 16 and 24 minutes
visual.caption: Each half-life takes the same time, whatever the starting concentration.

slides.narration: Here the concentration starts at nought point six four, falls to nought point three two after eight minutes, to nought point one six after sixteen, and to nought point nought eight after twenty four. Each halving takes the same eight minutes, wherever we start. A constant half-life is the signature of a first-order reaction.

slides.heading: Half-life of a first-order reaction
slides.body_md: Put $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0/2$ in the integrated equation: $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log 2 = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$. The half-life — and $k$ — are **independent of the initial concentration**. After $n$ half-lives, $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0/2^n$.

visual.alt: Table comparing zero- and first-order half-lives

slides.narration: Setting the concentration to half its starting value in the integrated equation gives the half-life: nought point six nine three divided by k. It contains no concentration, so the half-life of a first-order reaction is the same whether we start with a little or a lot. After n half-lives, the concentration has fallen to one over two to the power n of its starting value.

slides.heading: Worked example: time for a given fraction to react
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A first-order reaction has $k = 0.0577\ \text{min}^{-1}$. Find (a) its half-life and (b) the time for 90% of the reactant to react.

**(a)** $t_{1/2} = 0.693 \div 0.0577 = 12.0\ \text{min}$.

**(b)** 90% reacted: $[\ce{R}]_0/[\ce{R}] = 10$; $t = \dfrac{2.303}{0.0577}\log 10 = \dfrac{2.303}{0.0577} = 39.9\ \text{min}$.

visual.alt: Table of fraction reacted against time for the first-order example

slides.narration: The half-life is nought point six nine three over nought point nought five seven seven, twelve minutes. For ninety percent to react, one tenth is left, so the ratio of starting to present concentration is ten, whose log is one. So the time is simply two point three zero three over k, about forty minutes. Notice that ninety nine percent takes exactly twice as long.

slides.heading: Worked example: a drug in the blood
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An antibiotic is removed from the blood by a first-order process with a half-life of 5 h. A patient receives a dose giving 80 mg per litre of blood. What is the concentration after 20 h, and what is k?

**Step 1.** $n = 20 \div 5 = 4$; $[\ce{R}] = 80 \div 2^4 = 5.0\ \text{mg L}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** $k = 0.693 \div 5 = 0.139\ \text{h}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Flow of the antibiotic halving every five hours

slides.narration: Twenty hours is four half-lives of five hours. Halving four times takes eighty milligrams per litre down to five. The rate constant is nought point six nine three divided by five, about nought point one four per hour. Doctors use exactly this kind of calculation to decide how often a dose must be repeated.

slides.heading: Quick check: half-life
slides.body_md: Use the half-life to decide the order or to find how much reactant remains.
slides.narration: Quick check. A half-life that does not depend on the starting concentration means first order.

slides.heading: Molecularity and order
slides.body_md: An **elementary reaction** occurs in a single step; a **complex reaction** occurs in several steps (its **mechanism**). **Molecularity** is the number of reacting species colliding in an elementary step.
columns:
**Order**

- Found by experiment
- Sum of powers in the rate law
- May be 0, a fraction or a whole number
- Defined for the overall reaction

**Molecularity**

- Theoretical, from the mechanism
- Number of species in one elementary step
- Always 1, 2 or (rarely) 3; never 0 or fractional
- Defined only for elementary steps

visual.alt: Table of unimolecular, bimolecular and termolecular elementary steps

slides.narration: Order and molecularity are easily confused. Order comes from experiment and can be zero or a fraction. Molecularity is simply the number of particles that collide in one elementary step, so it is always one, two or, rarely, three. Three-particle collisions are rare because three molecules seldom meet at the same instant with the right energy and orientation.

slides.heading: Mechanism and the rate-determining step
slides.body_md: In a complex reaction, the **slowest elementary step** controls the overall rate: the **rate-determining step**. The rate law follows from it.

nodes.label: Rate = k[NO₂]², zero order in CO

visual.alt: Flow of a two-step mechanism with a slow first step

slides.narration: Most reactions take place in several steps, like a queue at a ticket counter followed by a quick security check: the slow step sets the pace. For nitrogen dioxide reacting with carbon monoxide at low temperature, the slow first step involves two nitrogen dioxide molecules, so the rate law is k times the square of nitrogen dioxide, and carbon monoxide does not appear at all.

slides.heading: Worked example: rate law from a mechanism
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The proposed mechanism for $\ce{2NO + Br2 -> 2NOBr}$ is: Step 1 (fast, equilibrium) $\ce{NO + Br2 <=> NOBr2}$; Step 2 (slow) $\ce{NOBr2 + NO -> 2NOBr}$. Deduce the rate law.

**Step 1.** Rate $= k_2[\ce{NOBr2}][\ce{NO}]$ (slow step).

**Step 2.** From the fast equilibrium, $[\ce{NOBr2}] = K[\ce{NO}][\ce{Br2}]$.

**Step 3.** Rate $= k_2K[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{Br2}] = k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{Br2}]$: third order overall.

visual.alt: Table of the two steps and their contributions to the rate law

slides.narration: Start from the slow step: the rate equals k two times the intermediate times nitric oxide. The intermediate cannot appear in the final rate law, so we use the fast equilibrium before it to replace it with K times nitric oxide times bromine. The result is second order in nitric oxide and first order in bromine, third order overall, which matches experiment.

slides.heading: Quick check: molecularity and mechanism
slides.body_md: Decide which statement about molecularity or the rate-determining step is correct.
slides.narration: Quick check. Molecularity is a small whole number for one elementary step; the slow step sets the rate law.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: log[R] against t is a straight line for first order; [R] against t for zero order.
Molecularity: species in one elementary step (1, 2, 3); order: experimental.
The slowest step of a mechanism determines the rate law.

visual.alt: Summary table of integrated rate equations and half-lives

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Integrating the rate law gives concentration against time: a straight line for zero order and an exponential decay for first order, whose half-life does not depend on the starting concentration. Molecularity counts the particles in one elementary step, while order is found by experiment, and the slowest step of a mechanism sets the rate law.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Use log (base 10) with the factor 2.303 consistently.
Half-life independent of [R]₀ → first order; proportional → zero order.
Eliminate intermediates from rate laws using a fast pre-equilibrium.

rows: t½ of first order depends on [R]₀

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Use common logs with the factor two point three zero three. When a percentage has reacted, the concentration left is the rest. Recognise the order from how the half-life behaves. And remember to remove intermediates from a rate law using the fast equilibrium step.

notes.title: Rate of Reaction and Rate Laws — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Rate of reaction
sections.body_md:
**Chemical kinetics** studies reaction rates, the factors that affect them and reaction mechanisms. **Ionic reactions** (e.g. Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl) are very fast because no bonds need breaking; **molecular reactions** are slower because covalent bonds must break.

**Average rate** $= -\Delta[\ce{R}]/\Delta t = \Delta[\ce{P}]/\Delta t$; **instantaneous rate** $= -d[\ce{R}]/dt$, found as minus the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve. For $\ce{aA + bB -> cC + dD}$: rate $= -\frac{1}{a}\frac{d[\ce{A}]}{dt} = -\frac{1}{b}\frac{d[\ce{B}]}{dt} = \frac{1}{c}\frac{d[\ce{C}]}{dt} = \frac{1}{d}\frac{d[\ce{D}]}{dt}$. Units: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

key_terms.definition_md: Change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, divided by its stoichiometric coefficient.
The rate at a particular moment, equal to minus the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve.

formulas.label: Rate in terms of each species

visual.alt: Concentration of a reactant falling along a curve from 0.6 towards zero over 50 seconds, with a straight tangent touching the curve at 15 seconds; the steepness of the tangent gives the instantaneous rate
visual.caption: Illustrative data. Instantaneous rate = −(slope of the tangent).

sections.heading: 2. Factors affecting rate; law of mass action
sections.body_md:
**Factors:** nature of reactants (ionic fast, covalent slower); surface area (powders faster); concentration or pressure (more collisions); temperature (rate roughly doubles per 10 K rise); catalyst (lower activation energy); radiation (photochemical reactions such as H₂ + Cl₂ in sunlight, photosynthesis, fading of dyes).

**Law of mass action** (Guldberg and Waage): at constant temperature, the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the **active masses** of the reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient. Active mass = molar concentration; for pure solids and liquids it is taken as 1. Strictly valid for elementary reactions.

key_terms.definition_md: Molar concentration of a substance; taken as unity for pure solids and liquids.
Rate is proportional to the product of the active masses of reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.

visual.alt: Table of factors and their effect on rate

sections.heading: 3. Rate law, order and units of k
sections.body_md:
**Rate law:** rate $= k[\ce{A}]^x[\ce{B}]^y$, with $x$, $y$ found **experimentally** (not from coefficients). **Rate constant** $k$: rate at unit concentrations; depends on temperature and catalyst, not on concentration. **Order** $= x + y$: may be 0, a whole number or a fraction.

**Method of initial rates:** compare runs in which only one concentration changes; rate ratio = (concentration ratio)ⁿ.

**Units of k:** $(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ — zero order mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; first order s⁻¹; second order L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; third order L² mol⁻² s⁻¹.

key_terms.definition_md: The proportionality constant in the rate law; equal to the rate when all concentrations are 1 mol L⁻¹.
The sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the experimental rate law.

visual.alt: Table of units of the rate constant

sections.heading: 4. Zero-order reactions
sections.body_md: Rate $= k$. Integrated: $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0 - kt$; $k = ([\ce{R}]_0 - [\ce{R}])/t$. Plot of [R] against t: straight line, slope $-k$. Half-life $t_{1/2} = [\ce{R}]_0/2k$ (proportional to initial concentration). Examples: decomposition of NH₃ on hot Pt at high pressure; enzyme reactions at saturation.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction whose rate is independent of reactant concentration.

visual.alt: Zero-order reaction: the concentration falls in a straight line from 0.50 mol per litre to zero at 25 minutes; the slope is minus k
visual.caption: k = 0.02 mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹ in this example.

sections.heading: 5. First-order reactions
sections.body_md:
**Derivation:** $-d[\ce{R}]/dt = k[\ce{R}]$ → $d[\ce{R}]/[\ce{R}] = -k\,dt$ → $\ln([\ce{R}]_0/[\ce{R}]) = kt$, so $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{[\ce{R}]}$ and $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0e^{-kt}$. Plot of log[R] against t: straight line, slope $-k/2.303$.

**Half-life:** $t_{1/2} = 0.693/k$, independent of $[\ce{R}]_0$; $k$ is also independent of initial concentration. After $n$ half-lives, $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0/2^n$. Time for 99.9% reaction ≈ $10\,t_{1/2}$.

Examples: radioactive decay, decomposition of N₂O₅, elimination of many drugs. **Pseudo-first-order:** one reactant in large excess (acid hydrolysis of an ester in water; inversion of cane sugar).

key_terms.definition_md: The time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its initial value.
A reaction of higher order that behaves as first order because one reactant is in large excess.

visual.alt: First-order decay: the concentration halves every 8 minutes, from 0.64 to 0.32, 0.16 and 0.08 at 8, 16 and 24 minutes
visual.caption: Each half-life takes the same time, whatever the starting concentration.

visuals.alt: For a first-order reaction, a graph of log of concentration against time is a straight line sloping down; its slope equals minus k divided by 2.303
visuals.caption: Illustrative: slope −0.03 min⁻¹, so k = 2.303 × 0.03 = 0.069 min⁻¹.

sections.heading: 6. Molecularity, mechanism and the rate-determining step
sections.body_md:
**Elementary reaction:** one step; **complex reaction:** several steps (mechanism). **Molecularity:** number of reacting species colliding in an elementary step — 1, 2 or (rarely) 3, never 0 or fractional; defined only for elementary steps. **Order:** experimental, for the overall reaction; may be 0 or fractional.

The **slowest step** is the **rate-determining step**; the rate law follows from it. Intermediates are eliminated using a fast pre-equilibrium. Example: NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ at low T: slow step 2NO₂ → NO₃ + NO gives rate = k[NO₂]².

key_terms.definition_md: The number of reacting species taking part in an elementary step.
The slowest step in a reaction mechanism, which controls the overall rate.

visual.alt: Table comparing order and molecularity

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing orders from the coefficients of the overall equation.
- Forgetting to divide rates by stoichiometric coefficients.
- Using the percentage reacted instead of the fraction remaining in first-order calculations.
- Saying the half-life of a first-order reaction depends on the initial concentration.
- Including an intermediate in the final rate law.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Derivation of the first-order equation (3 marks): differential rate law, integration with limits, final form.
- Numericals: equation, substitution with units, answer with units of k or time.
- Initial-rate problems: order with respect to each reactant with reasoning, rate law, k with units.

questions.stem_md: In the contact process, 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃. If SO₃ is formed at 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, oxygen is used up at:
questions.solution_md: −d[O₂]/dt = ½ d[SO₃]/dt = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student plots [H₂O₂] against time for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. The instantaneous rate at 10 minutes is obtained from:

options.text_md: minus the slope of the tangent to the curve at 10 minutes
the slope of the line joining the first and last points
the concentration at 10 minutes divided by 10
the area under the curve up to 10 minutes

questions.solution_md: The instantaneous rate is −d[H₂O₂]/dt, the negative of the tangent’s slope at that time — option (a). A chord gives an average rate (b).

questions.stem_md: Barium chloride and sodium sulfate solutions give a white precipitate the instant they are mixed, whereas a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen needs a spark to react. The precipitation is fast because:

options.text_md: barium sulfate has a very high molar mass
free Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions combine on collision without breaking covalent bonds
precipitation reactions have a high activation energy

questions.solution_md: Ionic reactions need no bond breaking, so they are very fast — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the decomposition of N₂O₅ at a fixed temperature, the rate of reaction stays constant from start to finish.
questions.solution_md: False. As N₂O₅ is used up its concentration falls, so the rate decreases with time (the reaction is first order).

questions.stem_md: In the isomerisation A → B, $[\ce{A}]$ falls from $0.50$ to $0.38\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ in $10\ \text{min}$. What is the average rate, in mol L⁻¹ min⁻¹?
questions.solution_md: Average rate $= -\dfrac{\Delta[\ce{A}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{0.50 - 0.38}{10} = 0.012$, so $0.012\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: For the decomposition 2NOCl(g) → 2NO(g) + Cl₂(g), chlorine is formed at 1.5 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Calculate the rate of disappearance of NOCl and the rate of the reaction.

answer.model_answer_md: Rate $= -\tfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\ce{NOCl}]}{dt} = \dfrac{d[\ce{Cl2}]}{dt} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. So $-\dfrac{d[\ce{NOCl}]}{dt} = 2 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Rate of reaction 1.5 × 10⁻³; NOCl 3.0 × 10⁻³.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with reference to a concentration–time graph for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, how the average rate between two times differs from the instantaneous rate at one time.

answer.model_answer_md: The average rate is the change in concentration divided by the time interval, i.e. minus the slope of the chord joining two points on the curve. The instantaneous rate at a given time is minus the slope of the tangent drawn to the curve at that time; it equals the average rate only over a vanishingly small interval.

questions.solution_md: Chord vs tangent.

questions.stem_md: Equal masses of zinc granules and zinc powder are added to separate beakers of the same dilute hydrochloric acid. The powder gives hydrogen much faster because:

options.text_md: powdered zinc is a different allotrope
the powder lowers the concentration of the acid
granules act as a catalyst poison
it has a much larger surface area in contact with the acid

questions.solution_md: More exposed surface means more collisions per second — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A mixture of hydrogen and chlorine can be kept in the dark for days, but explodes when exposed to bright sunlight. The factor responsible is:

options.text_md: radiation (light), which starts a photochemical reaction

questions.solution_md: Light supplies the energy to split Cl₂ and start the chain reaction — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Treating 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) as a single elementary step, the law of mass action gives the rate as proportional to:
questions.solution_md: Each active mass is raised to its stoichiometric coefficient — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the decomposition CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), the active mass of solid calcium carbonate is:

options.text_md: equal to its mass in grams
equal to its number of moles

questions.solution_md: The concentration of a pure solid does not change, so its active mass is taken as 1 — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The law of mass action correctly predicts the rate law of H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr from its balanced equation.

**Reason (R):** For complex reactions, the order with respect to each reactant must be found by experiment.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false — the experimental rate law is k[H₂][Br₂]^½, not k[H₂][Br₂]; R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: State the law of mass action and explain what is meant by the active mass of (a) a gas in a closed vessel and (b) a pure solid such as iron in the Haber process.

answer.model_answer_md: At constant temperature, the rate of a reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient. (a) For a gas, the active mass is its molar concentration (moles per litre). (b) For a pure solid, the concentration is constant, so its active mass is taken as 1.

questions.solution_md: Statement; concentration; unity.

marking_scheme.step: Active mass of gas and solid

questions.stem_md: Explain, using one everyday example for each, how (a) temperature, (b) a catalyst and (c) surface area affect the rate of a reaction.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Raising the temperature increases the kinetic energy of molecules, so more collisions exceed the activation energy; the rate roughly doubles for each 10 K rise — food spoils faster outside a refrigerator. (b) A catalyst provides an alternative path of lower activation energy — enzymes such as amylase speed up digestion of starch. (c) A larger surface area exposes more particles to collision — coal dust burns explosively while a lump of coal burns slowly.

questions.solution_md: Three factors with examples.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the law of mass action. What is meant by active mass? [2]

(b) Explain how each of the following affects the rate of a reaction, giving one example: (i) nature of reactants, (ii) concentration, (iii) radiation. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) At constant temperature, the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient. Active mass is the molar concentration of a substance; for pure solids and liquids it is taken as unity. (b) (i) Ionic reactions such as AgNO₃ + NaCl are almost instantaneous because no bonds are broken, while molecular reactions such as the oxidation of CO are slower because covalent bonds must break. (ii) Higher concentration increases the number of collisions per second, so the rate increases, e.g. charcoal burns faster in pure oxygen than in air. (iii) Light supplies energy to start photochemical reactions, e.g. H₂ and Cl₂ react explosively in sunlight; photosynthesis needs light.

questions.solution_md: Law and active mass; three factors.

questions.stem_md: The rate constant for the decomposition of N₂O₅ in carbon tetrachloride at 318 K is 6.2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. The order of the reaction is:
questions.solution_md: A rate constant in s⁻¹ means first order — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For 2NO(g) + Br₂(g) → 2NOBr(g), doubling [NO] at constant [Br₂] makes the initial rate four times larger. The order with respect to NO is:
questions.solution_md: 2ⁿ = 4 gives n = 2 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The rate constant of the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide changes when:

options.text_md: the initial concentration of H₂O₂ is doubled
the volume of solution is doubled
the reaction has been running for some time

questions.solution_md: k depends on temperature (and catalyst), not on concentration — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The experimental rate law for H₂(g) + Br₂(g) → 2HBr(g) is rate = k[H₂][Br₂]^½. The overall order is:
questions.solution_md: 1 + ½ = 1.5 — option (a); the coefficients would wrongly give 2 (b).

questions.stem_md: For 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. If the volume of the reaction vessel is suddenly halved at constant temperature, the rate becomes:
questions.solution_md: Halving the volume doubles every concentration: 2² × 2 = 8 — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The order of a reaction can be a fraction.

**Reason (R):** Order is determined by experiment and need not be equal to the stoichiometric coefficients.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The order of the reaction 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ can be read directly from its balanced equation as two.
questions.solution_md: False. The reaction is experimentally first order; orders cannot be read from coefficients.

questions.stem_md: In the rate law rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ, the sum x + y is called the ___ of the reaction.
questions.solution_md: The **order** (overall order).

questions.stem_md: For rates measured in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, match the order of reaction with the unit of its rate constant.
questions.solution_md: Unit of k = (mol L⁻¹)^(1−n) s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: For 2A + B → C at 300 K: with [A] = 0.10 M and [B] = 0.10 M the initial rate is 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ M s⁻¹; with [A] = 0.20 M, [B] = 0.10 M it is 1.2 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; with [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.20 M it is 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ M s⁻¹. Find the rate constant, in L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4: second order in A. Doubling [B] has no effect: zero order in B. Rate $= k[\ce{A}]^2$; $k = 3.0 \times 10^{-4} \div 0.10^2 = 0.030$, so $0.030\ \text{L mol}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: The rate law for the oxidation of nitric oxide, 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, is rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. How does the rate change if (a) [NO] is tripled at constant [O₂], and (b) the volume of the vessel is doubled?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Rate is multiplied by 3² = 9. (b) Doubling the volume halves both concentrations, so the rate is multiplied by (½)² × ½ = ⅛.

questions.stem_md: For the reaction X + 2Y → products, initial rates were: [X] 0.05 M, [Y] 0.05 M: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M s⁻¹; [X] 0.10 M, [Y] 0.05 M: 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ M s⁻¹; [X] 0.05 M, [Y] 0.15 M: 1.8 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹. Deduce the rate law and calculate k with its unit.

answer.model_answer_md: Runs 1 and 2: [X] doubles, rate doubles → first order in X. Runs 1 and 3: [Y] triples, rate ×9 → second order in Y. Rate $= k[\ce{X}][\ce{Y}]^2$ (third order). $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \div (0.05 \times 0.05^2) = 1.6\ \text{L}^2\ \text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: k[X][Y]²; k = 1.6 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: Order in Y and rate law

questions.stem_md: Starting from rate = k[A]ⁿ, derive the units of the rate constant for zero, first and second order reactions when concentration is in mol L⁻¹ and time in seconds.

answer.model_answer_md: $k = \text{rate}/[\ce{A}]^n$, so the unit is $(\text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}) \div (\text{mol L}^{-1})^n = (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1-n}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. Zero order ($n = 0$): mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. First order ($n = 1$): s⁻¹. Second order ($n = 2$): L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: General expression and three cases.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between the average rate and the instantaneous rate of a reaction, and explain how each is found from a concentration–time graph. [2]

(b) For A + B → products: [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.20 M gives an initial rate of 4.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; [A] = 0.30 M, [B] = 0.20 M gives 1.2 × 10⁻² M s⁻¹; [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.40 M gives 4.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹. Deduce the rate law, calculate k with its unit, and find the rate when [A] = 0.25 M and [B] = 0.50 M. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Average rate is the change in concentration over a time interval, minus the slope of the chord between two points on the curve. Instantaneous rate is the rate at one moment, minus the slope of the tangent at that point.

(b) Tripling [A] triples the rate → first order in A; doubling [B] has no effect → zero order in B. Rate $= k[\ce{A}]$; $k = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \div 0.10 = 0.040\ \text{s}^{-1}$. Rate $= 0.040 \times 0.25 = 0.010\ \text{M s}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Chord vs tangent; rate = k[A], k = 0.040 s⁻¹; 0.010 M s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: The half-life of the decomposition of ammonia on a hot tungsten wire doubles when the initial pressure of ammonia is doubled. The reaction is:
questions.solution_md: For zero order t½ = [R]₀/2k, proportional to the initial amount — option (b).

questions.stem_md: For the zero-order decomposition of a gas on a saturated metal surface, which plot is a straight line?

options.text_md: Rate against the square of concentration
Concentration of the gas against time

questions.solution_md: [R] = [R]₀ − kt is linear in t with slope −k — option (d). log[R] vs t is linear for first order (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The half-life of a zero-order reaction, such as the decomposition of NH₃ on platinum at high pressure, is independent of the initial concentration.
questions.solution_md: False. For zero order t½ = [R]₀/2k, which is proportional to the initial concentration.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The decomposition of ammonia on hot platinum is zero order at high pressure.

**Reason (R):** Platinum is a transition metal.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A; the reaction is zero order because the platinum surface is fully covered with ammonia — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A zero-order reaction has $k = 0.050\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$. How long, in minutes, does it take for the reactant concentration to fall from $0.80$ to $0.20\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$?
Explain why the decomposition of ammonia on a hot platinum surface is zero order at high pressure but becomes first order at low pressure.

answer.model_answer_md: At high pressure the platinum surface is completely covered by adsorbed ammonia, so the rate depends only on the surface area, not on the gas pressure: zero order. At low pressure only part of the surface is covered, and the amount adsorbed (and so the rate) is proportional to the pressure of ammonia: first order.

questions.solution_md: Saturated vs partly covered surface.

marking_scheme.step: High pressure: surface saturated, zero order
Low pressure: rate ∝ pressure, first order

questions.stem_md: Derive the integrated rate equation and the half-life for a zero-order reaction R → P, and state the slope of the straight-line plot.

answer.model_answer_md: Rate $= -\dfrac{d[\ce{R}]}{dt} = k$, so $d[\ce{R}] = -k\,dt$. Integrating from $[\ce{R}]_0$ at $t = 0$ to $[\ce{R}]$ at $t$: $[\ce{R}] - [\ce{R}]_0 = -kt$, i.e. $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0 - kt$. At $t_{1/2}$, $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0/2$, so $t_{1/2} = [\ce{R}]_0/2k$. A plot of [R] against t is a straight line with slope $-k$.

questions.solution_md: Integration; half-life; slope −k.

questions.stem_md: Phosphorus-32, used to trace nutrient uptake in plants, decays by first-order kinetics with a half-life of 14.3 days. What fraction of a sample remains after 42.9 days?
questions.solution_md: 42.9 ÷ 14.3 = 3 half-lives; (½)³ = 0.125 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The decomposition of sulfuryl chloride, SO₂Cl₂ → SO₂ + Cl₂, is first order with a half-life of 693 s at a certain temperature. Its rate constant is:
For the first-order decomposition of N₂O₅, a graph of log[N₂O₅] against time is a straight line with slope:
questions.solution_md: log[R] = log[R]₀ − kt/2.303 — option (c). Slope −k applies to ln[R] (a).

questions.stem_md: The acid-catalysed inversion of cane sugar, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆, behaves as a first-order reaction because:

options.text_md: water is present in such large excess that its concentration stays practically constant
water does not take part in the reaction
the reaction is elementary and unimolecular

questions.solution_md: The rate k[sucrose][H₂O] becomes k′[sucrose] — a pseudo-first-order reaction — option (a).

questions.stem_md: After three half-lives of the first-order decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in a bottle, the percentage of H₂O₂ that has decomposed is:
questions.solution_md: Remaining (½)³ = 12.5%, so 87.5% has decomposed — option (a); 12.5% is the amount left (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The half-life of the first-order decomposition of N₂O₅ is the same whether the initial concentration is 0.1 M or 0.5 M.

**Reason (R):** For a first-order reaction, t½ = 0.693/k.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A: the expression contains no concentration term — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A first-order reaction has $k = 2.31 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. How long, in seconds, does it take for 75% of the reactant to be consumed?
A patient’s blood contains $60\ \text{mg L}^{-1}$ of a drug that is eliminated by first-order kinetics with $k = 0.115\ \text{h}^{-1}$. What is the concentration, in mg L⁻¹, after 12 hours?
Show that, for a first-order reaction such as the decay of a radioactive tracer, the time required for 99.9% of the reactant to react is about ten times its half-life.
questions.solution_md: Ratio ≈ 10.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the acid hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate in a large excess of water is called a pseudo-first-order reaction. Write its rate law.

answer.model_answer_md: The true rate law is rate $= k[\ce{CH3COOC2H5}][\ce{H2O}]$, second order. Water is in such large excess that its concentration hardly changes, so $k[\ce{H2O}]$ is a constant $k'$ and rate $= k'[\ce{CH3COOC2H5}]$: it behaves as first order.

questions.solution_md: Excess water; k′.

marking_scheme.step: True rate law and excess water

questions.stem_md: Derive the integrated rate equation for a first-order reaction R → P and show that its half-life is independent of the initial concentration.

answer.model_answer_md: $-\dfrac{d[\ce{R}]}{dt} = k[\ce{R}]$, so $\dfrac{d[\ce{R}]}{[\ce{R}]} = -k\,dt$. Integrating between $[\ce{R}]_0$ at $t = 0$ and $[\ce{R}]$ at $t$: $\ln[\ce{R}] - \ln[\ce{R}]_0 = -kt$, so $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{[\ce{R}]}$. At $t_{1/2}$, $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0/2$: $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log 2 = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$, which contains no concentration term.

questions.solution_md: Integration; t½ = 0.693/k.

questions.stem_md: In the first-order decomposition of N₂O₅ in carbon tetrachloride, [N₂O₅] falls from 0.040 M to 0.010 M in 40 minutes. Calculate (a) the rate constant, (b) the half-life and (c) the concentration after a further 20 minutes.
Two reactions, one zero order and one first order, both start at 0.40 M and have a half-life of 10 minutes. Calculate the concentration remaining in each after 20 minutes, and explain the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: Zero order: $t_{1/2} = [\ce{R}]_0/2k$ gives $k = 0.40 \div 20 = 0.020\ \text{M min}^{-1}$; after 20 min, $[\ce{R}] = 0.40 - 0.020 \times 20 = 0$ (complete). First order: two half-lives, $[\ce{R}] = 0.40 \div 4 = 0.10\ \text{M}$. A zero-order reaction loses a constant amount per minute, so the second half takes as long as the first; a first-order reaction slows as concentration falls, losing half of what remains in each half-life.

questions.solution_md: 0 M vs 0.10 M.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Derive the integrated rate equation for a first-order reaction and obtain the expression for its half-life. [3]

(b) The half-life of a first-order reaction is 40 minutes. Calculate (i) the time for the concentration to fall to one-tenth of its initial value and (ii) the fraction remaining after 2 hours. [2]
questions.solution_md: Derivation; 133 min; 1/8.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Compare zero-order and first-order reactions with respect to (i) the straight-line plot, (ii) the unit of k and (iii) the dependence of half-life on initial concentration. [3]

(b) A zero-order reaction with [R]₀ = 0.60 M has a half-life of 15 min. Calculate k and the time for complete reaction. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) Zero order: [R] against t is linear (slope −k); first order: log[R] against t is linear (slope −k/2.303). (ii) Zero order: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; first order: s⁻¹. (iii) Zero order: $t_{1/2} = [\ce{R}]_0/2k$, proportional to [R]₀; first order: $t_{1/2} = 0.693/k$, independent of [R]₀.

(b) $k = [\ce{R}]_0/2t_{1/2} = 0.60 \div 30 = 0.020\ \text{M min}^{-1}$; complete when $[\ce{R}] = 0$: $t = 0.60 \div 0.020 = 30\ \text{min}$.

questions.solution_md: Comparison; k = 0.020 M min⁻¹; 30 min.

questions.stem_md: The step NO(g) + O₃(g) → NO₂(g) + O₂(g) is elementary. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text_md: It is bimolecular and its rate law is rate = k[NO][O₃]
It is unimolecular because only NO is oxidised
Its order must be found by experiment and could be zero
It is termolecular because four molecules appear in the equation

questions.solution_md: Two species collide in the elementary step, so it is bimolecular and the rate law follows its stoichiometry — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The mechanism proposed for 2NO₂Cl → 2NO₂ + Cl₂ is: NO₂Cl → NO₂ + Cl (slow); NO₂Cl + Cl → NO₂ + Cl₂ (fast). The rate law is:
questions.solution_md: The slow first step is unimolecular in NO₂Cl and controls the rate — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Termolecular steps such as 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ are rare because:

options.text_md: three molecules can never react together
three particles seldom collide at the same instant with enough energy and the right orientation

questions.solution_md: The chance of a simultaneous effective three-body collision is very small — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The molecularity of an elementary step is always a whole number.

**Reason (R):** Molecularity can be found only by experiment.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false — molecularity is a theoretical count of colliding species from the mechanism; it is order that is experimental — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A complex reaction such as the iodide-catalysed decomposition of H₂O₂ has a single molecularity for the overall reaction.
questions.solution_md: False. Molecularity is defined only for each elementary step; the overall reaction has an order, not a molecularity.

questions.stem_md: In a reaction mechanism, the slowest elementary step, which controls the overall rate, is called the ___ step.
questions.solution_md: The **rate-determining** step.

questions.stem_md: For the two-step mechanism NO + Br₂ ⇌ NOBr₂ (fast); NOBr₂ + NO → 2NOBr (slow), match each term with its example from this mechanism.
questions.solution_md: NOBr₂ is formed and used up; the slow step controls the rate and is bimolecular; rate = k[NO]²[Br₂] is third order.

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between the order and the molecularity of a reaction, using the decomposition of N₂O₅ (experimentally first order) as an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Order is found by experiment and refers to the overall reaction; molecularity is the number of species colliding in an elementary step. Order may be zero or fractional; molecularity is always 1, 2 or 3. For 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ the order is 1, although two molecules appear in the overall equation; molecularity can be stated only for its individual steps.

questions.solution_md: Two differences with example.

marking_scheme.step: Experimental vs theoretical / overall vs step

questions.stem_md: The decomposition of ozone, 2O₃ → 3O₂, is thought to occur by: O₃ ⇌ O₂ + O (fast equilibrium, constant K); O + O₃ → 2O₂ (slow). Derive the rate law and state the order with respect to O₃ and O₂.

answer.model_answer_md: Slow step: rate $= k_2[\ce{O}][\ce{O3}]$. From the fast equilibrium, $K = \dfrac{[\ce{O2}][\ce{O}]}{[\ce{O3}]}$, so $[\ce{O}] = \dfrac{K[\ce{O3}]}{[\ce{O2}]}$. Rate $= k_2K\dfrac{[\ce{O3}]^2}{[\ce{O2}]} = k\dfrac{[\ce{O3}]^2}{[\ce{O2}]}$: second order in O₃, order −1 in O₂ (overall first order).

questions.solution_md: k[O₃]²/[O₂].

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by the rate-determining step? Give two differences between order and molecularity. [2]

(b) For 2NO₂Cl → 2NO₂ + Cl₂, the proposed mechanism is: step 1 (slow) NO₂Cl → NO₂ + Cl; step 2 (fast) NO₂Cl + Cl → NO₂ + Cl₂. (i) Identify the intermediate. (ii) State the molecularity of each step. (iii) Write the rate law and the overall order. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The slowest elementary step in a mechanism, which controls the overall rate. Order is found by experiment and may be zero or fractional; molecularity is the number of species in an elementary step and is always a whole number (1, 2 or 3). (b) (i) Cl (chlorine atom), formed in step 1 and used in step 2. (ii) Step 1 is unimolecular; step 2 is bimolecular. (iii) The slow step controls the rate: rate = k[NO₂Cl], first order overall.

questions.solution_md: RDS; differences; Cl; uni/bi; k[NO₂Cl].
